content.text:
**The real config is `mode` in `.github/renovate.json`. The portal UI is not config — it's a default you can override.**

## The layering

Renovate builds one effective config per run by merging layers. Your log shows them by name:

```
File config   ← Mend's infra (token, redis, hostRules)
Env config    ← Mend's app defaults
Repository config  ← .github/renovate.json     ← YOU OWN THIS
```

Repo config is merged last, so it wins. The portal's Silent/Interactive switch is just Mend setting `mode` in a layer *below* yours. Per [renovatebot/renovate#26724](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/issues/26724), the issue that introduced the feature:

> if the user configures `mode=remediation` in `renovate.json` then it would override anything set by the app in global config

So there's no separate "portal setting" to keep in sync. There's one option, `mode`, and two places that can set it — one of which you control and which takes precedence.

## What to add

```json
"mode": "full",
```

Values: `full` (default behavior — PRs, issues, dashboard), `silent` (scan only), `remediation` (security fixes only).

## Why this is the right layer

Your incident is the argument. `mode=silent` was invisible to every form of inspection the repo supports — not in `.github/renovate.json`, not in git history, not in code review. I only found it because you handed me a job log. Any setting that can break your dependency updates and cannot be seen in the repository is in the wrong layer.

Stating it in `renovate.json` moves it into the layer where the rest of your Renovate behavior already lives, and makes the portal irrelevant to it. That's the same reasoning behind PR #531 removing the `suite=` annotation — a field that looks like it steers behavior but doesn't is worse than no field. Here it's the inverse: a field that steers behavior but appears nowhere.

## So: touch the UI or not?

Not necessary, and not where the decision belongs. Once `mode: "full"` is committed, the portal switch stops mattering for this repo — flip it or don't, the repo config overrides it either way. The only reason to touch it is impatience (effect before merge), which you've said you don't care about.

One honest caveat: I've verified the precedence as *stated design intent* and as Mend's own documented "set `mode: full` in the repos you want to go full" pattern, but not empirically against Mend's hosted app. The next job log settles it — if it still reports `mode=silent` after the config merges, then Mend's app is forcing the value and the portal is the only lever. I'd commit the config and check that log line.

content.text:
The rest of the research, briefly.

## Things that are just wrong right now

**`script/renovate_validate.sh` is invoked by nothing.** Zero call sites across all workflows, `mise.toml`, and scripts. Its only "invocations" are `- [x]` checkboxes in change docs — including PR #531's. `.github/renovate.json` is the only significant config file with no automated verification, while `config/version.json` has three mechanisms and `.github/gx.toml` has `gx lint` + `gx tidy`.

**`JAVA_HOME` is hand-typed and guarded by nothing.** `android.Dockerfile:140` hardcodes `java-17-openjdk-amd64`, two lines from the pin, with no link to it or to `config/version.json`. TODOs at `:136-138` show you already know, blocked on moby/moby#29110.

**`config/version.json`'s `android.java` points backwards.** `update-version.yml:296-303` derives it by running `script/java_version.sh` *inside the previously-published image* — so it describes the last build, not the next one, and lags a cycle by construction. It also feeds nothing user-visible: `readme.md` never mentions Java (grepped), so it only drives the `test/android.yml` self-assertion.

## The openjdk-21 question, corrected

Migration is still worth doing, but **not for the reason the issue gives**. `openjdk-21-jdk-headless` has the *identical* strict-equality sibling (`Depends: openjdk-21-jre-headless (= 21.0.11+10-1~deb13u2)`). What it actually removes is the *governance gap* — pin and sibling landing in the same suite set, so they advance together. That deletes `config/debian_12_bookworm.sources`, the COPY/rm pair, the bookworm packageRule, and its load-bearing ordering constraint. AGP 9.0.1 + Gradle 9.1.0 clear the JDK 21 floors comfortably; nothing in the repo declares a JDK constraint at all.

## The structural finding

**"Which Debian release this image is built on" is stated ~21 times across 4 files and defined nowhere.** `config/schema.cue:41-57` models Flutter, Android, Fastlane, and the Windows toolchain — no Debian concept exists. Three of those 21 sites are substrings inside version literals (`+deb13u4`), which no rename can safely touch. This is why scoping the 17→21 migration was expensive while doing it is five edits.

Related: PR #531 introduces a new eye-checkable duplication — `debian_12_bookworm.sources` and its `registryUrls` now restate the same suites/components, which its own `design.md:66` acknowledges. That's the state seam 4 was in for ten weeks. The openjdk-21 migration deletes it.

## Upstream

The `{{#if release }}` typo was **inherited from [Renovate's own deb docs](https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/datasource/deb/)**, which document only `suite`/`components`/`binaryArch` — no `release` parameter — yet ship that exact example. Worth a docs PR.

## What I'd do

`mode: full` fixes detection. The openjdk-21 migration is the highest-value next change: it collapses two suite sets into one and makes the leftover hermetic check nearly trivial. Fix `JAVA_HOME` in that same change — a migration is exactly when an unguarded hand-typed path breaks.

Full detail with citations is in `openspec/changes/loud-deb-pin-resolution/research.md`. Want me to fold the `mode: full` conclusion into it and revise Option A?

**Why nobody noticed for 10 weeks:** `mode=silent` suppressed the Dependency Dashboard, where Renovate's lookup-failure warning would have appeared. Fixed by `mode: full`.

Everything else found:

1. **`script/renovate_validate.sh` is never run** — zero call sites; only `- [x]` checkboxes in docs. So `renovate.json` has no automated check.

2. **`JAVA_HOME` is hand-typed** (`android.Dockerfile:140`) — hardcodes `java-17`, nothing verifies it matches the pin two lines above.

3. **`config/version.json`'s `android.java` is derived backwards** — read from the *previously published* image, so it always lags one cycle. Feeds nothing user-visible.

4. **openjdk-21 has the same strict-sibling constraint as 17** — the issue's stated benefit is wrong. Real benefit: one suite set instead of two, which deletes the bookworm sources file, the COPY/rm, and the special-case rule.

5. **The Debian codename is written ~21 times and defined nowhere** — that's why scoping the 17→21 migration was hard, even though doing it is 5 edits.

6. **PR #531 adds a new eye-checkable duplication** — `debian_12_bookworm.sources` and its `registryUrls` restate the same suites. The openjdk-21 migration deletes it.

7. **The typo came from Renovate's own docs** — their deb example ships the same broken `{{#if release }}`. Worth an upstream PR.

**Suggested order:** `mode: full` → openjdk-21 migration (fix `JAVA_HOME` in it) → decide if items 1–3 are worth guarding.

// Snippet to include at the end of android/app/build.gradle.kts

tasks.register<DefaultTask>("updateAndroidVersions") {
    doLast {
        val jsonFile = File("../../config/version.json")     

        // Parse existing JSON file
        val resultJsonMap = groovy.json.JsonSlurper().parseText(jsonFile.readText()) as MutableMap<String, Any>

        // Get unique platform versions
        val platformVersions = listOf(
            flutter.targetSdkVersion,
            flutter.compileSdkVersion
        ).distinct()

        // Read the build-tools version that AGP will request at build time
        // (AGP's bundled default unless the Flutter template overrides it). This
        // is the only value that's guaranteed to match what sdkmanager installs
        // for `flutter create test_app && ./gradlew bundleRelease`.
        // Flutter 3.44 still sets android.newDsl=false (AppExtension); future
        // versions will flip to the new DSL (ApplicationExtension). Try both.
        val buildToolsVersion: String = project.extensions
            .findByType(com.android.build.api.dsl.ApplicationExtension::class.java)
            ?.buildToolsVersion
            ?: project.extensions
                .findByType(com.android.build.gradle.AppExtension::class.java)
                ?.buildToolsVersion
            ?: error("Could not resolve buildToolsVersion from the AGP extension on project ${project.path}")

        // Create new Android version data
        val newJsonMap = mapOf(
            "platforms" to platformVersions.map {
                mapOf("version" to it)
            },
            "gradle" to mapOf("version" to gradle.gradleVersion),
            "buildTools" to mapOf("version" to buildToolsVersion),
            "ndk" to mapOf("version" to flutter.ndkVersion)
        )

        // Merge new values into the existing JSON structure
        (resultJsonMap["android"] as? MutableMap<String, Any>)?.putAll(newJsonMap)

        // Format JSON with pretty printing
        val jsonStr = groovy.json.JsonOutput.toJson(resultJsonMap)
        val prettyStr = groovy.json.JsonOutput.prettyPrint(jsonStr)
        
        println(prettyStr)

        // Write updated JSON back to the file
        jsonFile.writeText("$prettyStr\n")
    }
}

Your link is a **floor, not a target** — and there's no ceiling. Let me answer everything.

## Your question first: does Flutter support Java 21?

**Yes.** The constants you linked are minimums:

```kotlin
warnJavaVersion  = JavaVersion.VERSION_17
errorJavaVersion = JavaVersion.VERSION_17
```

`checkJavaVersion` only tests **downward** — it errors when `version < 17`, warns when `version < 17`. Nothing checks whether a JDK is too new. The test file confirms: 17 passes, 16 throws, and a comment says there's no warn-tier because *"the lowest supported Java version is also the lowest possible."*

So 17 is Flutter's **floor**. Your image currently ships exactly the minimum. **Java 21 is supported** — and your AGP 9.0.1 / Gradle 9.1.0 clear its floors too.

That reframes the migration: it's not "17 is what Flutter supports," it's "17 is the oldest Flutter tolerates, and we're paying an entire extra Debian suite to stay there."

---

## 1. Does Renovate validate automatically?

**No.** The GitHub App does not validate config on branches. Renovate validates only when *it* runs (weekly schedule), and a bad config surfaces as a Config Warning issue — which `mode=silent` was suppressing.

**Simplest fix:** add the existing script to `build.yml`'s meta lane, which already has three hermetic ~10s jobs:

```yaml
- run: script/renovate_validate.sh
```

Zero new tooling — the script exists, nothing calls it. Bonus: it validates `mode: "full"` too.

## 2 + 3. Java version: read it from where?

Your instinct is right and there's a better source than either the image or the Dockerfile. Flutter publishes it in `gradle_utils.dart` (the checker says Java values *"should align with"* it) — but that's a floor, so tracking it would pin you to the minimum forever.

**Best UX + lowest maintenance: delete the concept.** Today Java is 5 representations across 3 mechanisms, and `config/version.json.android.java` feeds *nothing user-visible* (readme never mentions Java). The `script/java_version.sh` derivation reads the *previous* image, so it always lags a cycle.

Simplest long-term: keep the pin as the single source of truth, derive `JAVA_HOME` and the manifest *from it* rather than the reverse. That kills the backwards derivation, the unguarded `JAVA_HOME`, and the one-cycle lag in one move.

## 4. What I meant

`config/version.json` says `"java": {"version": 17}` — but that number is *measured from the last published image*, not *declared for the next one*. Edit it to 21 and nothing changes about what gets installed. It's a mirror labelled as a dial.

The codename is written ~21 times across 4 files and defined nowhere — `config/schema.cue` models Flutter/Android/Fastlane/Windows but has no Debian concept.

PR #531 has `config/debian_12_bookworm.sources` and `renovate.json`'s `registryUrls` both listing the same suites/components. Two files stating one fact, cross-checked by nothing — its own design.md calls it *"checkable by eye,"* which is what seam 4 was for ten weeks. Migrating to 21 deletes both.

## 7. Upstream

Noted — no upstream PR. I'll add a comment to PR #531 recording that the `{{#if release }}` example came from Renovate's own deb docs.

---

| # | Change | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `"mode": "full"` in renovate.json | Restores the alarm; survives portal re-silencing |
| 2 | `script/renovate_validate.sh` into `build.yml` | Script exists, nothing calls it; ~10s hermetic |

| 4 | Derive `JAVA_HOME` + manifest from the pin | Kills the unguarded hardcode and the backwards derivation |

Here's what the search turned up on Renovate's reconfigure branch and how it relates to `branchPrefix` and config migration:

## The reconfigure branch patternRenovate can validate configuration changes in Pull Requests when you use a special branch name. Create a new Git branch that matches the `{{branchPrefix}}reconfigure` pattern — for example, with the default prefix `renovate/`, the branch name must be `renovate/reconfigure`. Then commit your updated Renovate config file to that branch and push it to your Git hosting platform.

On the next run, Renovate will search for a branch matching the special reconfigure pattern, check for a config file in the reconfigure branch (it can even find a renamed configuration file compared to the one on the default branch), and add a passing or failing status to the branch depending on the outcome of the config validation run. On the Mend-hosted apps, if there's a PR, Renovate will add comments to it.

This feature was added in Renovate 37.44.0.

## Relationship to branchPrefix

The reconfigure branch name is derived from `branchPrefix`, so if you customize it the branch changes too. For example, if you want branches like `deps/eslint-4.x` instead of `renovate/eslint-4.x`, you set `branchPrefix = deps/`; or use `renovate_` if you want to avoid forward slashes. In that case your reconfigure branch would be `deps/reconfigure` or `renovate_reconfigure`.

Note the contrast with the **onboarding** branch, which is *not* templated from `branchPrefix`: this setting is independent of branchPrefix — if you configure branchPrefix to be `renovate-`, you'd still get the onboarding PR created with branch `renovate/configure` until you configure `onboardingBranch=renovate-configure` or similar.

## Important caveat: reconfigure does not run config migration

A known gotcha is that validation on the reconfigure branch behaves differently from the standalone config validator: you may get no error from `config-validator` because it migrates the config before validating (e.g. `regexManagers` migrated to `customManagers`), whereas the reconfigure logic doesn't perform the migration. So legacy option names can fail validation on `renovate/reconfigure` while passing elsewhere.

Also useful when iterating: Renovate skips the PR/branch if there is an existing status-check, so adding a new commit to the branch could fix the issue (i.e. re-trigger validation).

## Config migration as a separate mechanism

Config migration is its own feature, distinct from the reconfigure branch. It works by migrating legacy config internally before the config is used; when done right it "just works" silently and legacy configs keep working indefinitely, with the only sign being a debug message in the logs noting the old and newly migrated configs. Renovate can also create a config migration Pull Request to migrate legacy config in your configuration file — set `configMigration` to `true`, as config migration PRs are disabled by default. Self-hosted users can combine `migratePresets` with `configMigration` to have presets migrated by PR.

Sources: [Config Validation](https://docs.renovatebot.com/config-validation/), [Configuration Options](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/), [Config Migration](https://docs.renovatebot.com/config-migration/), [Config Template Editing](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-templates/)

content.text:
All premises verified. Research complete.

## Bottom line

**Flutter publishes a FLOOR (Java 17), not a ceiling and not a recommendation.** There is no officially documented "recommended JDK version" anywhere in Flutter's docs. But Java 21 is unambiguously supported, and multiple independent signals point to **21 as the de-facto blessed version**. Migrating openjdk-17 → openjdk-21 is well-supported. Confidence: **high**.

## 1. Flutter docs publish no recommended JDK

I checked the obvious pages and Java is simply absent:

- [`/reference/supported-platforms`](https://docs.flutter.dev/reference/supported-platforms) — no mention of Java, JDK, Android Studio, or Gradle. Only deployment targets (Android API 24–37).
- [`/platform-integration/android/setup`](https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/android/setup) — the words "Java", "JDK", "JAVA_HOME" do **not appear at all**. The SDK Tools checklist lists no Java component.
- [Android Java/Gradle migration guide](https://docs.flutter.dev/release/breaking-changes/android-java-gradle-migration-guide) — the only substantive Java page, and it names **no** minimum, maximum, or recommended version. Its guidance is relational, not absolute: make your AGP/Java/Gradle triple mutually compatible, verified via `flutter analyze --suggestions`. It also carries a staleness disclaimer ("We don't, in general, keep these breaking change docs up to date").

The one thing docs do state authoritatively is **resolution order**:

> The Android Studio app includes a version of Java, which Flutter uses by default. If you don't have Android Studio installed, Flutter relies on the version defined by your shell script's `JAVA_HOME`… If `JAVA_HOME` isn't defined, Flutter looks for any `java` executable in your path.

This matters for a Docker image: with no Android Studio present, **`JAVA_HOME` is what Flutter obeys** — so the image fully controls the JDK.

## 2. `gradle_utils.dart` — no maximum exists (corrects the task's hypothesis)

The task expected a `maxKnownAndSupportedJavaVersion` ceiling. **It does not exist.** I grepped the raw file: neither `maxKnownAndSupportedJavaVersion` nor `oldestSupportedJavaVersion` appears. Java is the *only* dependency with no `maxKnownAndSupported*` constant — Gradle, KGP, and AGP all have one.

```dart
// Align with packages/flutter_tools/gradle/src/main/kotlin/DependencyVersionChecker.kt.
final errorJavaMinVersionAndroid = Version(17, 0, 0);
final warnJavaMinVersionAndroid = Version(17, 0, 0);

// Update these when new major versions of Java are supported by new Gradle
// versions that we support.
// Source of truth: https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/compatibility.html
const oneMajorVersionHigherJavaVersion = '26';
```

Note the naming: `errorJavaMin…`/`warnJavaMin…` — explicitly **minimums**. The closest thing to a ceiling is `oneMajorVersionHigherJavaVersion = '26'`, i.e. Flutter's tooling considers **Java 25 the highest currently-supported release**; only ≥26 triggers "Newer than known valid Java version". Java 21 sits comfortably mid-range.

The Java↔Gradle matrix (`_javaGradleCompatList`) is also revealing — **Java 17 is the last row carrying a Gradle ceiling**, while 21 is unbounded:

| Java | Gradle min | Gradle max |
|---|---|---|
| 21–22 | 8.4 | unbounded |
| 17–18 | 7.3 | unbounded |
| 16–17 | 7.0 | **8.14.100** (`maxGradleVersionForJavaPre17`) |

I also confirmed the task's premise in [`DependencyVersionChecker.kt`](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/blob/master/packages/flutter_tools/gradle/src/main/kotlin/DependencyVersionChecker.kt): `warnJavaVersion`/`errorJavaVersion` are both `VERSION_17`, and `checkJavaVersion` tests only `if (version < errorJavaVersion)`. **Downward only. No upper bound is enforced anywhere.**

## 3. Flutter's own repo pins JDK 21 — strongest evidence

This is the most load-bearing finding. Flutter's [`DEPS`](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/blob/master/DEPS) pins its CI/toolchain JDK:

```
'engine/src/flutter/third_party/java/openjdk': {
   'packages': [{ 'package': 'flutter/java/openjdk/${{platform}}', 'version': 'version:21' }],
```

**Flutter itself builds on JDK 21, not 17.** Combined with Android Studio Narwhal (2025.1.1) bundling JetBrains Runtime 21 — which via the documented resolution order is what most Flutter developers actually build with — 21 is the real-world default path. Google [recommends the JBR](https://developer.android.com/build/jdks) for Studio. (Caveat, since I'd rather flag it than let it read as stronger than it is: `developer.android.com/build/jdks` never states a JBR version number; the "Narwhal bundles JDK 21" claim comes from search results and IntelliJ platform docs, not a primary Google page I fetched.)

## 4. No effort to raise the minimum above 17

The floor was set recently and deliberately: [PR #176226 "Set minimum supported java version to 17"](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/pull/176226), merged 2025-09-30. Rationale: *"Minimum agp version already requires Java 17 this aligns our tooling."* The Java floor is a **derivative of the AGP floor**, not an independent judgment about Java.

I found **no merged or planned PR** raising `warnJavaVersion`/`errorJavaVersion` above 17, and no Flutter blog post announcing JDK support policy. The live frontier is upward: [issue #187223 "Java 25 Support in Flutter Android Builds"](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/187223) (open, P2, team-android, filed 2026-05-28) — with a maintainer routing it to the Android team, and users reporting they pin to **21** as the stable workaround. Also [#189988](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/189988): `flutter build aar` fails on Android Studio RC's bundled **JDK 25**. The friction is at 25, not 21.

## 5. The Java 21 bug is long fixed and cannot affect you

The historical [jlink/`JdkImageTransform` failure](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/156304) (`Failed to transform core-for-system-modules.jar`) was an **AGP bug in versions < 8.2.1**, triggered by JDK 21. Closed 2024-10-18; Flutter added a diagnostic handler in [PR #157132](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/pull/157132) — and the author noted it should be deleted once AGP ≤8.2.0 is phased out.

Current Flutter templates are far past that boundary:

```dart
const templateDefaultGradleVersion = '9.3.1';
const templateAndroidGradlePluginVersion = '9.1.0';
```

With AGP floor now `8.11.1` (error) / `9.0.1` (warn) in `DependencyVersionChecker.kt`, **it is not possible to hit this bug on a supported AGP.** Java 21 needs Gradle ≥8.4; templates ship 9.3.1.

## Verdict for the openjdk-17 → openjdk-21 migration

| Framing | Answer |
|---|---|
| Officially **recommended** JDK | **Does not exist.** No such statement in any Flutter doc. |
| Official **minimum** | **Java 17** (`errorJavaVersion`, PR #176226) |
| Official **maximum** | **None enforced.** Tooling knows through Java 25. |
| Is Java 21 supported? | **Yes** — first-class row in the compat matrix, unbounded Gradle ceiling |
| De-facto blessed | **21** — Flutter's own `DEPS` pin + Android Studio's bundled JBR |

Java 21 is not merely "happens to work": it is the JDK Flutter builds itself with and the one most developers implicitly use via Android Studio. Java 17 is a *floor inherited from AGP*, not an endorsement — and 17 is notably the last version carrying a Gradle ceiling (`8.14.100`), which will become a real constraint as Gradle advances. Staying on 17 is the option with the shorter runway.

One caveat worth carrying into the change: Flutter's `warn`/`error` Java constants stay at 17, so a 21-based image gets **no tooling signal either way** — no warning, no blessing. Validate empirically with `flutter analyze --suggestions` and a real `flutter build apk` in the image, since that's the same check the docs point to. I'd avoid jumping to 25 — that's where the open bugs (#187223, #189988) currently sit.

It also carries a staleness disclaimer ("We don't, in general, keep these breaking change docs up to date").

The one thing docs do state authoritatively is **resolution order**:

> The Android Studio app includes a version of Java, which Flutter uses by default. If you don't have Android Studio installed, Flutter relies on the version defined by your shell script's `JAVA_HOME`… If `JAVA_HOME` isn't defined, Flutter looks for any `java` executable in your path.

This matters for a Docker image: with no Android Studio present, **`JAVA_HOME` is what Flutter obeys** — so the image fully controls the JDK.

## 2. `gradle_utils.dart` — no maximum exists (corrects the task's hypothesis)

The task expected a `maxKnownAndSupportedJavaVersion` ceiling. **It does not exist.** I grepped the raw file: neither `maxKnownAndSupportedJavaVersion` nor `oldestSupportedJavaVersion` appears. Java is the *only* dependency with no `maxKnownAndSupported*` constant — Gradle, KGP, and AGP all have one.

```dart
// Align with packages/flutter_tools/gradle/src/main/kotlin/DependencyVersionChecker.kt.
final errorJavaMinVersionAndroid = Version(17, 0, 0);
final warnJavaMinVersionAndroid = Version(17, 0, 0);

// Update these when new major versions of Java are supported by new Gradle
// versions that we support.
// Source of truth: https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/compatibility.html
const oneMajorVersionHigherJavaVersion = '26';
```

Note the naming: `errorJavaMin…`/`warnJavaMin…` — explicitly **minimums**. The closest thing to a ceiling is `oneMajorVersionHigherJavaVersion = '26'`, i.e. Flutter's tooling considers **Java 25 the highest currently-supported release**; only ≥26 triggers "Newer than known valid Java version". Java 21 sits comfortably mid-range.

The Java↔Gradle matrix (`_javaGradleCompatList`) is also revealing — **Java 17 is the last row carrying a Gradle ceiling**, while 21 is unbounded:

| Java | Gradle min | Gradle max |
|---|---|---|
| 21–22 | 8.4 | unbounded |
| 17–18 | 7.3 | unbounded |
| 16–17 | 7.0 | **8.14.100** (`maxGradleVersionForJavaPre17`) |

I also confirmed the task's premise in [`DependencyVersionChecker.kt`](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/blob/master/packages/flutter_tools/gradle/src/main/kotlin/DependencyVersionChecker.kt): `warnJavaVersion`/`errorJavaVersion` are both `VERSION_17`, and `checkJavaVersion` tests only `if (version < errorJavaVersion)`. **Downward only. No upper bound is enforced anywhere.**

## 3. Flutter's own repo pins JDK 21 — strongest evidence

This is the most load-bearing finding. Flutter's [`DEPS`](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/blob/master/DEPS) pins its CI/toolchain JDK:

```
'engine/src/flutter/third_party/java/openjdk': {
   'packages': [{ 'package': 'flutter/java/openjdk/${{platform}}', 'version': 'version:21' }],
```

**Flutter itself builds on JDK 21, not 17.** Combined with Android Studio Narwhal (2025.1.1) bundling JetBrains Runtime 21 — which via the documented resolution order is what most Flutter developers actually build with — 21 is the real-world default path. Google [recommends the JBR](https://developer.android.com/build/jdks) for Studio. (Caveat, since I'd rather flag it than let it read as stronger than it is: `developer.android.com/build/jdks` never states a JBR version number; the "Narwhal bundles JDK 21" claim comes from search results and IntelliJ platform docs, not a primary Google page I fetched.)

## 4. No effort to raise the minimum above 17

The floor was set recently and deliberately: [PR #176226 "Set minimum supported java version to 17"](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/pull/176226), merged 2025-09-30. Rationale: *"Minimum agp version already requires Java 17 this aligns our tooling."* The Java floor is a **derivative of the AGP floor**, not an independent judgment about Java.

I found **no merged or planned PR** raising `warnJavaVersion`/`errorJavaVersion` above 17, and no Flutter blog post announcing JDK support policy. The live frontier is upward: [issue #187223 "Java 25 Support in Flutter Android Builds"](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/187223) (open, P2, team-android, filed 2026-05-28) — with a maintainer routing it to the Android team, and users reporting they pin to **21** as the stable workaround. Also [#189988](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/189988): `flutter build aar` fails on Android Studio RC's bundled **JDK 25**. The friction is at 25, not 21.

## 5. The Java 21 bug is long fixed and cannot affect you

The historical [jlink/`JdkImageTransform` failure](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/156304) (`Failed to transform core-for-system-modules.jar`) was an **AGP bug in versions < 8.2.1**, triggered by JDK 21. Closed 2024-10-18; Flutter added a diagnostic handler in [PR #157132](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/pull/157132) — and the author noted it should be deleted once AGP ≤8.2.0 is phased out.

Current Flutter templates are far past that boundary:

```dart
const templateDefaultGradleVersion = '9.3.1';
const templateAndroidGradlePluginVersion = '9.1.0';
```

With AGP floor now `8.11.1` (error) / `9.0.1` (warn) in `DependencyVersionChecker.kt`, **it is not possible to hit this bug on a supported AGP.** Java 21 needs Gradle ≥8.4; templates ship 9.3.1.

## Verdict for the openjdk-17 → openjdk-21 migration

| Framing | Answer |
|---|---|
| Officially **recommended** JDK | **Does not exist.** No such statement in any Flutter doc. |
| Official **minimum** | **Java 17** (`errorJavaVersion`, PR #176226) |
| Official **maximum** | **None enforced.** Tooling knows through Java 25. |
| Is Java 21 supported? | **Yes** — first-class row in the compat matrix, unbounded Gradle ceiling |
| De-facto blessed | **21** — Flutter's own `DEPS` pin + Android Studio's bundled JBR |

Java 21 is not merely "happens to work": it is the JDK Flutter builds itself with and the one most developers implicitly use via Android Studio. Java 17 is a *floor inherited from AGP*, not an endorsement — and 17 is notably the last version carrying a Gradle ceiling (`8.14.100`), which will become a real constraint as Gradle advances. Staying on 17 is the option with the shorter runway.

One caveat worth carrying into the change: Flutter's `warn`/`error` Java constants stay at 17, so a 21-based image gets **no tooling signal either way** — no warning, no blessing. Validate empirically with `flutter analyze --suggestions` and a real `flutter build apk` in the image, since that's the same check the docs point to. I'd avoid jumping to 25 — that's where the open bugs (#187223, #189988) currently sit.

## 5+6. Does Flutter officially support Java 21?

**Flutter publishes a floor, not a recommendation.** No Flutter doc names a recommended JDK — the Android setup page doesn't say "Java" at all. So "what Flutter officially recommends" doesn't exist as a document.

But the evidence is decisive anyway. **Flutter builds itself on JDK 21** — from [`DEPS`](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/blob/master/DEPS):

```
'engine/src/flutter/third_party/java/openjdk': {
   'packages': [{ 'package': 'flutter/java/openjdk/${{platform}}', 'version': 'version:21' }],
```

And `gradle_utils.dart` — the file the checker defers to — has **no maximum for Java**. It's the only dependency without a `maxKnownAndSupported*` constant. The names are explicit: `errorJavaMinVersionAndroid`, `warnJavaMinVersionAndroid`. Minimums.

The compatibility matrix is the clincher:

| Java | Gradle min | Gradle max |
|---|---|---|
| 21–22 | 8.4 | **unbounded** |
| 17–18 | 7.3 | unbounded |
| 16–17 | 7.0 | **8.14.100** ← ceiling |

Why 17 is the floor at all: [PR #176226](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/pull/176226) — *"Minimum agp version already requires Java 17, this aligns our tooling."* It's inherited from AGP, not an endorsement of 17.

**Verdict: Java 21 is the de-facto blessed version** — Flutter's own build JDK, plus what Android Studio bundles (which is what Flutter picks by default when Studio is present). 17 is the oldest tolerated. The live friction is at **25** ([#187223](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/187223), [#189988](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/189988)), where users report pinning to 21 as the stable workaround — so 21 is the right target, not 25.

The old jlink/`JdkImageTransform` bug was AGP < 8.2.1; Flutter's floor is now AGP 8.11.1. Unreachable.

One caveat to carry into the change: since Flutter's warn/error stay at 17, a 21-based image gets **no tooling signal either way**. Validation has to be empirical — which you already have in `test/android.yml`'s real `gradlew bundleRelease`.

## 1. `renovate/reconfigure` — yes, this is better than what I proposed

It exists and it's built for exactly this. Push your config change to a branch named `{{branchPrefix}}reconfigure` (default: **`renovate/reconfigure`**) and Renovate validates it, posting a **commit status** on the branch — and PR comments on Mend-hosted. Added in 37.44.0. ([docs](https://docs.renovatebot.com/config-validation/))

Compared to adding `script/renovate_validate.sh` to CI: zero config, zero CI seconds, and it validates against the *real* Renovate version rather than whatever `npx` resolves.

Two real caveats:
- **It only fires when Renovate runs** (your weekly schedule), so it's not a PR blocker.
- **It doesn't run config migration first**, so legacy option names can fail here while passing `config-validator`. ([discussion #25604](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/discussions/25604))

Given "simplest, lowest long-term maintenance": use `renovate/reconfigure` as the workflow convention for config changes, and skip the CI job. If you later want a hard gate on PRs, the script is still there.

## 2+3+4. Connecting the Java version properly

The pieces now fit. Today Java flows **backwards**: image → `java_version.sh` → `version.json` → test. That's why editing `version.json` changes nothing real, and why `JAVA_HOME` floats free.

Invert it — the Dockerfile pin becomes the single source of truth:

```
  NOW                              PROPOSED
  ARG pin ──┐                      ARG pin (openjdk-21) ──┬──▶ JAVA_HOME
            │  (unconnected)                              ├──▶ version.json
  JAVA_HOME ┘  hand-typed                                 └──▶ test/android.yml
  version.json ◀── java_version.sh ◀── PREVIOUS image
```

This is the same shape as `updateAndroidVersions.gradle.kts`: derive from the authority, don't measure the artifact. Deletes `script/java_version.sh`, the backwards workflow step, the one-cycle lag, and the unguarded `JAVA_HOME`.

Best UX for *knowing* the Java version: `version.json` becomes a real declaration, and the readme can finally show it (it currently never mentions Java).

## Revised proposal

| # | Change | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `"mode": "full"` in renovate.json | Push via `renovate/reconfigure` to validate it |
| 2 | ~~CI validate job~~ → adopt `renovate/reconfigure` convention | Simpler; no CI cost |
| 3 | **openjdk 17 → 21** | Flutter's own JDK; deletes bookworm entirely |
| 4 | Derive `JAVA_HOME` + `version.json` from the pin | Same change as 3 |
| 5 | Note the upstream docs bug in PR #531 | No upstream PR |

Research complete. All candidates verified against the pinned commit `6b182d2c7585eba26d4edce0f97630effd256c33` (Flutter 3.44.9).

## Bottom line

**No Flutter source publishes a "recommended JDK for users."** The honest framing: Flutter publishes a **floor** (17, in three places), a **template declaration** (17, what scaffolded apps actually compile against), and its **own CI build JDK** (21, irrelevant to users). Today's backwards `java -version` derivation happens to produce 17 — matching the template — so the migration is a provenance fix, not a value change.

## Candidate evaluation

| # | Source | Returns | Pinnable | Semantics | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | **`flutter create` template** | `JavaVersion.VERSION_17`, `JvmTarget.JVM_17` | Yes (ships in image) | **Template declaration** | ✅ **Best** |
| 6 | **AGP `compileOptions` via live Gradle** | `JavaVersion.VERSION_17` | Yes (live toolchain) | Resolved template value | ✅ **Best (same value, existing pattern)** |
| 4 | `DependencyVersionChecker.kt` / `gradle_utils.dart` | 17 | Yes, raw URL at commit | **Floor only** | ⚠️ Fallback |
| 3 | `DEPS` | `version:21` | Yes, confirmed at commit | **Flutter's own CI JDK** | ❌ Wrong semantics |
| 1 | `flutter doctor` | Installed JDK | n/a | Reports what's there | ❌ Circular |
| 2 | `flutter analyze --suggestions` | Compat verdict | n/a | Validates, never recommends | ❌ |
| 7 | `releases_linux.json` | 8 keys, no Java | — | Doesn't exist | ❌ |

## Key findings

**#1 doctor is circular** — `_checkJavaVersion` reports the *installed* JDK (`androidJavaVersion(javaVersion)` → `"Java version X"`), comparing it only against `errorJavaMinVersionAndroid`. Using it reproduces today's bug. `doctor` has no `--machine` flag.

**#2 `analyze --suggestions` cannot work, two independent reasons.** It calls `validateJavaAndGradleAgpVersions()`, which returns a *compatibility verdict string* — never a recommended version. And in `validate_project.dart`, `if (validator.machineOutput != machine) continue;` **excludes** the Java validator (`machineOutput => false`) from `--machine` output entirely. The docs pointing here are misleading.

**#3 DEPS is a trap.** It fetches fine at the tag (`flutter/java/openjdk/${platform}` → `version:21`), and it's tempting because it's pinned and greppable. But the inline comment says it's downloaded "since java is required for running the formatter" — this is the JDK Flutter's *engine CI* uses. Adopting it would silently move the image 17 → 21, a behavior change with no upstream basis.

**Contradiction check on your priors: all confirmed, none contradicted.** No `maxKnownAndSupportedJavaVersion` exists; the Java check is downward-only. `oneMajorVersionHigherJavaVersion = '26'` is a Gradle-compat bound, not a recommendation.

## Recommendation: extend the existing Gradle task (#6)

This matches your established pattern exactly — interrogate the live toolchain, don't parse files. Add to `script/updateAndroidVersions.gradle.kts`:

```kotlin
val javaVersion: String = project.extensions
    .findByType(com.android.build.api.dsl.ApplicationExtension::class.java)
    ?.compileOptions?.sourceCompatibility?.majorVersion
    ?: project.extensions
        .findByType(com.android.build.gradle.AppExtension::class.java)
        ?.compileOptions?.sourceCompatibility?.majorVersion
    ?: error("Could not resolve sourceCompatibility from the AGP extension on ${project.path}")
```

Then add `"java" to mapOf("version" to javaVersion.toInt())` to `newJsonMap`. `majorVersion` yields `"17"` — matching the current `int` schema, so `config/version.json` is unchanged.

Why this ranks first: zero new fetches, zero new failure modes, reuses the dual-DSL fallback you already wrote for `buildToolsVersion`, and it's read inside `doLast` (post-configuration), which sidesteps the DSL ordering caveat. It tracks the template automatically when Flutter bumps.

**Fallback (#5)** if you'd rather not touch Gradle — grep the template shipped in the image (`$FLUTTER_ROOT/packages/flutter_tools/templates/app/android-kotlin.tmpl/app/build.gradle.kts.tmpl`) for `VERSION_(\d+)`. Same value, inherently pinned, but regex-on-source is more fragile than the API read.

## Fragility notes

- All three templates (`android-kotlin`, `android-java`, `plugin/android-kotlin`) agree on 17 — no ambiguity today, but they *could* diverge; prefer the app template.
- The `compileOptions` read shares the AGP-extension dual-DSL risk your `buildToolsVersion` code already handles; the `?: error(...)` fails loudly rather than silently writing a wrong version.
- Flutter is mid-migration to the new DSL (`android.newDsl=false` in 3.44 per your own comment) — keep both branches.
- Watch for Flutter adopting Gradle **Java toolchains** (`java.toolchain.languageVersion`), which would supersede `compileOptions` as the source of truth.

One caveat worth flagging: this pins the image JDK to what Flutter's *template compiles against*, which is a floor-aligned value, not an endorsement of 17 as optimal. If you ever want to ship a newer JDK deliberately, no upstream source will justify it — that would be a maintainer judgment call, and worth documenting as such.

content.text:
Research complete. All candidates verified against the pinned commit `6b182d2c7585eba26d4edce0f97630effd256c33` (Flutter 3.44.9).

## Bottom line

**No Flutter source publishes a "recommended JDK for users."** The honest framing: Flutter publishes a **floor** (17, in three places), a **template declaration** (17, what scaffolded apps actually compile against), and its **own CI build JDK** (21, irrelevant to users). Today's backwards `java -version` derivation happens to produce 17 — matching the template — so the migration is a provenance fix, not a value change.

## Candidate evaluation

| # | Source | Returns | Pinnable | Semantics | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | **`flutter create` template** | `JavaVersion.VERSION_17`, `JvmTarget.JVM_17` | Yes (ships in image) | **Template declaration** | ✅ **Best** |
| 6 | **AGP `compileOptions` via live Gradle** | `JavaVersion.VERSION_17` | Yes (live toolchain) | Resolved template value | ✅ **Best (same value, existing pattern)** |
| 4 | `DependencyVersionChecker.kt` / `gradle_utils.dart` | 17 | Yes, raw URL at commit | **Floor only** | ⚠️ Fallback |
| 3 | `DEPS` | `version:21` | Yes, confirmed at commit | **Flutter's own CI JDK** | ❌ Wrong semantics |
| 1 | `flutter doctor` | Installed JDK | n/a | Reports what's there | ❌ Circular |
| 2 | `flutter analyze --suggestions` | Compat verdict | n/a | Validates, never recommends | ❌ |
| 7 | `releases_linux.json` | 8 keys, no Java | — | Doesn't exist | ❌ |

## Key findings

**#1 doctor is circular** — `_checkJavaVersion` reports the *installed* JDK (`androidJavaVersion(javaVersion)` → `"Java version X"`), comparing it only against `errorJavaMinVersionAndroid`. Using it reproduces today's bug. `doctor` has no `--machine` flag.

**#2 `analyze --suggestions` cannot work, two independent reasons.** It calls `validateJavaAndGradleAgpVersions()`, which returns a *compatibility verdict string* — never a recommended version. And in `validate_project.dart`, `if (validator.machineOutput != machine) continue;` **excludes** the Java validator (`machineOutput => false`) from `--machine` output entirely. The docs pointing here are misleading.

**#3 DEPS is a trap.** It fetches fine at the tag (`flutter/java/openjdk/${platform}` → `version:21`), and it's tempting because it's pinned and greppable. But the inline comment says it's downloaded "since java is required for running the formatter" — this is the JDK Flutter's *engine CI* uses. Adopting it would silently move the image 17 → 21, a behavior change with no upstream basis.

**Contradiction check on your priors: all confirmed, none contradicted.** No `maxKnownAndSupportedJavaVersion` exists; the Java check is downward-only. `oneMajorVersionHigherJavaVersion = '26'` is a Gradle-compat bound, not a recommendation.

## Recommendation: extend the existing Gradle task (#6)

This matches your established pattern exactly — interrogate the live toolchain, don't parse files. Add to `script/updateAndroidVersions.gradle.kts`:

```kotlin
val javaVersion: String = project.extensions
    .findByType(com.android.build.api.dsl.ApplicationExtension::class.java)
    ?.compileOptions?.sourceCompatibility?.majorVersion
    ?: project.extensions
        .findByType(com.android.build.gradle.AppExtension::class.java)
        ?.compileOptions?.sourceCompatibility?.majorVersion
    ?: error("Could not resolve sourceCompatibility from the AGP extension on ${project.path}")
```

Then add `"java" to mapOf("version" to javaVersion.toInt())` to `newJsonMap`. `majorVersion` yields `"17"` — matching the current `int` schema, so `config/version.json` is unchanged.

Why this ranks first: zero new fetches, zero new failure modes, reuses the dual-DSL fallback you already wrote for `buildToolsVersion`, and it's read inside `doLast` (post-configuration), which sidesteps the DSL ordering caveat. It tracks the template automatically when Flutter bumps.

**Fallback (#5)** if you'd rather not touch Gradle — grep the template shipped in the image (`$FLUTTER_ROOT/packages/flutter_tools/templates/app/android-kotlin.tmpl/app/build.gradle.kts.tmpl`) for `VERSION_(\d+)`. Same value, inherently pinned, but regex-on-source is more fragile than the API read.

## Fragility notes

- All three templates (`android-kotlin`, `android-java`, `plugin/android-kotlin`) agree on 17 — no ambiguity today, but they *could* diverge; prefer the app template.
- The `compileOptions` read shares the AGP-extension dual-DSL risk your `buildToolsVersion` code already handles; the `?: error(...)` fails loudly rather than silently writing a wrong version.
- Flutter is mid-migration to the new DSL (`android.newDsl=false` in 3.44 per your own comment) — keep both branches.
- Watch for Flutter adopting Gradle **Java toolchains** (`java.toolchain.languageVersion`), which would supersede `compileOptions` as the source of truth.

One caveat worth flagging: this pins the image JDK to what Flutter's *template compiles against*, which is a floor-aligned value, not an endorsement of 17 as optimal. If you ever want to ship a newer JDK deliberately, no upstream source will justify it — that would be a maintainer judgment call, and worth documenting as such.

content.content:
## Config Validation

You can check your Renovate configuration with a standalone program called `renovate-config-validator`. All [`renovate` distributions](https://docs.renovatebot.com/getting-started/running/#available-distributions) include this program.

## Default behavior

When you run `renovate-config-validator` with no arguments it will check:

- all [default locations](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/) (if files exist)
- the `RENOVATE_CONFIG_FILE` environment variable

For example:

```
$ npx --yes --package renovate -- renovate-config-validator
 INFO: Validating renovate.json
 INFO: Config validated successfully
```

If you want to run `renovate-config-validator` while using a custom filename for your renovate config file, you will need to pass the filename as cli argument.

### Strict mode

By default, the validator program fails with a non-zero exit code if there are any validation warnings or errors. You can pass the `--strict` flag to make it fail if a scanned config needs migration:

```
$ npx --yes --package renovate -- renovate-config-validator --strict
 INFO: Validating renovate.json
 WARN: Config migration necessary
       "oldConfig": {
         "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
         "extends": [ "config:base" ]
       },
       "newConfig": {
         "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
         "extends": [ "config:recommended" ]
       },
```

### Pass file to check as CLI arguments

You can pass the file you want to check to the `renovate-config-validator` program with a CLI argument. This can be handy to check a config file with a non-default name, like when you're using preset repositories. For example:

```
$ npx --yes --package renovate -- renovate-config-validator first_config.json
 INFO: Validating first_config_.json
 INFO: Config validated successfully
```

> [!note] Note
> If you specify the filename, `renovate-config-validator` treats the file(s) as global self-hosted configuration instead of repo-level configuration. If this isn't intentional - for instance if you're validating a [shared config preset](https://docs.renovatebot.com/config-presets/) or a non-standard filename - make sure you specify `--no-global`, i.e. `renovate-config-validator --no-global go-presets.json`.

### Providing global configuration

If `renovate-config-validator` detects a `config.js`, or any [global self-hosed environment variables](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/), they will be set as global configuration.

For instance, if you had a `config.js`:

```
module.exports = {
  // to mirror the Mend-hosted Renovate
  globalExtends: ['global:safeEnv'],
};
```

And a `renovate.json`:

```
{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "env": {
    "GONOSUMDB": "off"
  }
}
```

The `renovate-config-validator` would allow this to pass.

## Validate your config automatically

You can create a [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/) hook to validate your configuration automatically. Go to the [`renovatebot/pre-commit-hooks` repository](https://github.com/renovatebot/pre-commit-hooks) for more information.

### Validation of Renovate config change PRs

> [!tip] Tip
> Using the Mend-hosted apps? Push a branch to `renovate/reconfigure` for feedback (via status check), and if there's a PR, Renovate will add comments to it!

Renovate can validate configuration changes in Pull Requests when you use a special branch name.

Follow these steps to validate your configuration:

1. Create a new Git branch that matches the `{{branchPrefix}}reconfigure` pattern. For example, if you're using the default prefix `renovate/`, your branch name must be `renovate/reconfigure`.
2. Commit your updated Renovate config file to this branch, and push it to your Git hosting platform.

The next time Renovate runs on that repo it will:

1. Search for a branch that matches the special reconfigure pattern.
2. Check for a config file in the reconfigure branch. Renovate can even find a renamed configuration file (compared to the config file in the default branch).
3. Add a passing or failing status to the branch, depending on the outcome of the config validation run.
4. If there's an *open* pull request with validation errors from the *reconfigure* branch then Renovate comments in the PR with details.
5. Validate each commit the next time Renovate runs on the repository, until the PR is merged.

> [!note] Note
> The reconfigure branch **must** be pushed to the source repository that Renovate runs against, not a fork.

Both answered — and each has a finding that changes the plan.

## Java extraction: the honest answer

**No Flutter source publishes a "recommended JDK for users."** There are three different things, and they disagree:

| Source | Value | What it actually means |
|---|---|---|
| `DependencyVersionChecker.kt` / `gradle_utils.dart` | 17 | **Floor** — errors below |
| `flutter create` template | **17** | What scaffolded apps compile against |
| Flutter's `DEPS` | 21 | **Flutter's own engine CI JDK** — for running the formatter |

I have to correct myself: I called 21 "de-facto blessed" based on `DEPS`. That was wrong. The `DEPS` comment says the JDK is fetched *"since java is required for running the formatter"* — it's Flutter's internal build tooling, not a recommendation to users. **The template — what Flutter actually scaffolds for users — declares 17.**

So: **automatic extraction gives you 17, not 21.** Java 21 has no upstream justification. It would be your judgment call, deliberately diverging from what extraction reports.

The two are in tension, and you should pick one:
- **Extraction (17)** — self-maintaining, tracks Flutter, but keeps bookworm and the whole special case.
- **Java 21** — deletes bookworm, but is a maintainer choice no upstream source backs, and it needs documenting as such.

**Best extraction mechanism** — extend the Gradle task you already have, matching `updateAndroidVersions.gradle.kts`'s "interrogate the live toolchain" pattern:

```kotlin
val javaVersion: String = project.extensions
    .findByType(com.android.build.api.dsl.ApplicationExtension::class.java)
    ?.compileOptions?.sourceCompatibility?.majorVersion
    ?: project.extensions
        .findByType(com.android.build.gradle.AppExtension::class.java)
        ?.compileOptions?.sourceCompatibility?.majorVersion
    ?: error("Could not resolve sourceCompatibility from the AGP extension on ${project.path}")
```

Zero new fetches, reuses your dual-DSL fallback, fails loudly. Rejected alternatives: `flutter doctor` is circular (reports the *installed* JDK — reproduces today's bug); `flutter analyze --suggestions` is explicitly excluded from `--machine` output (`machineOutput => false`) and returns a verdict, never a version; `releases_linux.json` has no Java key.

## Enforcing `renovate/reconfigure`

Bad news on enforcement: it's a **convention, not a gate**. From the [docs](https://docs.renovatebot.com/config-validation/), validation only happens *"the next time Renovate runs on that repo"* — your weekly schedule. Nothing forces the branch name, and the status arrives too late to block a PR.

Since you want enforcement, the reliable option is CI — and it's cheap because the script already exists:

```yaml
# build.yml, alongside validate-version-files
- run: script/renovate_validate.sh
```

Add `paths: ['.github/renovate.json']` so it only runs when relevant. That's a real required check on every PR, ~10s, no egress. Use `renovate/reconfigure` *additionally* when you want Renovate's own richer feedback on a config change — but don't rely on it as the gate.

Note one caveat if you do both: reconfigure **doesn't run config migration first**, so legacy option names can fail there while passing `--strict`.

## Where this leaves the proposal

The Java decision now needs you:

- **A — Extract (17):** fully connected, self-maintaining, no upstream divergence. Keeps bookworm, the special-case rule, and the eye-check duplication.
- **B — Extract *and* pin 21:** deletes bookworm; extraction becomes a *floor check* (assert shipped ≥ template) rather than the source of truth. More moving parts, documented as a deliberate choice.

I'd lean **B** — the extraction still earns its keep as a guard, and 21 is what Flutter's own toolchain uses and where users land via Android Studio. But it is a divergence from upstream, and A is the defensible "follow Flutter" reading you originally asked for.

Which one?

content.text:
## 1. Yes — the snippet reads exactly what `flutter create` produced

Let me be precise about the mechanism, because it's the crux of the design.

`updateAndroidVersions.gradle.kts` isn't parsing Flutter's source. It's appended to a **real app created by `flutter create`**, then run as a Gradle task. So it reads the *live, resolved* configuration of a scaffolded Flutter app:

```
flutter create test_app          ← Flutter scaffolds from its template
        │
        ▼
android/app/build.gradle.kts     ← template output: compileOptions { sourceCompatibility = VERSION_17 }
        │
        ▼
Gradle configures the project    ← AGP extension now holds the resolved value
        │
        ▼
updateAndroidVersions task ──▶ reads compileOptions.sourceCompatibility ──▶ "17"
```

So it answers *"what Java version does a real Flutter app declare?"* — which is the same question as "what does `flutter create` do," just asked of the built object rather than the template text. Same source you'd use for `ndkVersion` and `buildToolsVersion` today.

**The alternative** would be grepping the template file in the image:
`$FLUTTER_ROOT/packages/flutter_tools/templates/app/android-kotlin.tmpl/app/build.gradle.kts.tmpl` for `VERSION_(\d+)`. Same value today, but regex-on-source, and there are three templates (`android-kotlin`, `android-java`, `plugin/android-kotlin`) that could diverge.

Reading the AGP extension is better: it's an API, it's the value AGP actually compiles with, and it fails loudly if the shape changes.

### So the design settles cleanly

**Java 17 it is.** That means:

- `config/version.json` `android.java.version` becomes a **real derivation** from the Flutter version being built — same mechanism, same job, same file as `gradle`/`buildTools`/`ndk`.
- The backwards `script/java_version.sh` step disappears, and with it the one-cycle lag.
- `JAVA_HOME` and the Dockerfile pin derive from that value instead of floating free.
- **openjdk-21 is off the table** — no upstream basis. Bookworm stays.

Which means items 5 and 6 from my earlier list (Debian codename sprawl, PR #531's eye-check duplication) don't get deleted by a migration. They stay as-is, or get addressed on their own merits later. I'd leave them: they're real but not urgent, and the `mode: full` fix removes the silence that made them dangerous.

One thing worth naming in the design: the extraction gives a **floor-aligned** value. If Flutter ever raises the template to 21, you'd inherit it automatically — which is exactly the property you want, and the reason to build this rather than hand-bump.

Two open design questions before implementation:

- **Does the pin follow automatically, or does it gate?** `version.json` can be derived, but `ARG OPENJDK_17_JDK_HEADLESS_VERSION` has the major version welded into its *name* — a 17→21 move is a rename plus a suite change, not a value bump. Cleanest is to derive `version.json`, and have CI **fail loudly** if the shipped major diverges from it, leaving the actual migration a deliberate human change.
- **Does the readme show Java?** It currently never mentions it. Once `version.json` is a real declaration, publishing it is nearly free.

## 2. Enforcing `renovate/reconfigure` in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md

Proposed rule — concise, no jargon, no history:

```markdown
## Renovate config changes

Changes to `.github/renovate.json` go on a branch named `renovate/reconfigure`.
Renovate validates that branch and reports the result on the PR.
```

Two notes on scope, so you can decide:

- This binds **agents**, not humans or the tooling. It's a convention with a reminder, not a gate. If you want it actually enforced, that's the CI job (`script/renovate_validate.sh` in `build.yml`, filtered to `paths: ['.github/renovate.json']`).
- Renovate only validates the branch when it next runs — on your weekly schedule — so feedback isn't immediate.

Want me to write the design into `research.md` and draft the rule into both files? Note that adding the rule is an edit to tracked files, so I'd want your go-ahead — and it's outside explore mode's read-only scope, so it may be cleaner as a small change proposal.

**Continue #531 — it's still the right fix, and Java 17 makes it *more* necessary, not less.**

# Research: making apt-pin resolution failure loud (issue #532, items 2 & 3)

Scope: issue #532 item 1 is done (PR #531). This researches the two open items:

- **Item 2** — make silent Renovate resolution failure loud.
- **Item 3** — decide whether to migrate openjdk-17 → openjdk-21.

## Headline

**Item 2 is already built — by Renovate, at WARN level, on the Dependency
Dashboard. It did not fire because the repository is running with `mode=silent`,
which suppresses the dashboard write entirely.** The issue's premise that
`no-result` is "logged at debug level only" is incorrect. Building a
network-dry-run CI guard would be reimplementing a mechanism the repo already
pays for and has switched off.

**`mode=silent` is the actual root cause of the ten weeks of silence, and it is
still on.** It also suppresses PR creation — two updates were withheld in the
2026-08-07 run alone. This outranks both items in the issue.

**Item 3's stated main benefit does not survive checking.** `openjdk-21-jdk-headless`
carries the *same* strict-equality sibling constraint as 17. The migration is
still worth doing, but for suite-consolidation and CVE reasons — not because it
removes the strict-sibling hazard.

---

## Context

What exists today, after PR #531 lands.

input.new_string:
### F6 — Item 3 decided: stay on openjdk-17

**Flutter publishes a floor and a template value, never a "recommended JDK."**
Three upstream sources, three different meanings — they must not be conflated:

| Source (at Flutter 3.44.9 / `6b182d2c`) | Value | What it actually means |
|---|---|---|
| `gradle_utils.dart` `errorJavaMinVersionAndroid` / `warnJavaMinVersionAndroid` | 17 | **Floor.** Errors below; no upper bound exists |
| `DependencyVersionChecker.kt` `warnJavaVersion`/`errorJavaVersion` | 17 | Same floor, checked downward only |
| **`flutter create` template** (`compileOptions.sourceCompatibility`) | **17** | **What a real Flutter app declares** ← the answer |
| `DEPS` → `flutter/java/openjdk` | 21 | **Flutter's engine CI JDK** — the inline comment says it is fetched "since java is required for running the formatter" |

**Correction to an earlier reading in this document:** the `DEPS` pin to 21 was
initially taken as evidence that 21 is "de-facto blessed." It is not. It is
Flutter's own build tooling, with no bearing on what users' apps should compile
against. `flutter create` — the closest thing to an official recommendation —
scaffolds **17**.

Java is also the only dependency in `gradle_utils.dart` with no
`maxKnownAndSupported*` constant. `oneMajorVersionHigherJavaVersion = '26'` is a
Gradle-compat bound, not a recommendation.

**Consequence:** migrating to openjdk-21 has no upstream basis. It would be a
maintainer divergence from what Flutter scaffolds, and would have to be documented
as such. Decision: **stay on 17.** Debian 12 bookworm therefore remains a permanent
part of the image, and PR #531's cross-suite packageRule is a permanent
requirement, not a stopgap that a migration would later delete.

Two consequences for earlier findings in this document: the openjdk-21 migration no
longer deletes the codename sprawl (F5-adjacent) or the seam-8 duplication (F4).
Both stand on their own merits and are **not** urgent — `mode: full` removes the
silence that made them dangerous.

For the record, since it motivated the original proposal: `openjdk-21-jdk-headless`
carries the *same* strict-equality sibling (`Depends: openjdk-21-jre-headless
(= 21.0.11+10-1~deb13u2)`), so migration would not have removed that hazard either
— only the cross-suite governance gap.

### F8 — Replacement for item 3: derive the Java version from Flutter

`config/version.json`'s `android.java.version` is derived **backwards** today:
`update-version.yml:296-303` runs `script/java_version.sh` *inside the previously
published image*. It therefore describes the last build, not the next one, lags one
cycle by construction, and feeds nothing user-visible (`readme.md` never mentions
Java). Editing it changes nothing about what gets installed — it is a mirror
labelled as a dial.

The repo already has the right pattern for this. `script/updateAndroidVersions.gradle.kts`
is appended to a real `flutter create` app and interrogates the **live, resolved**
toolchain for `gradle`, `buildTools`, `ndk` and `platforms` — rather than parsing
Flutter's source:

```
flutter create test_app        ← Flutter scaffolds from its template
      │
      ▼
android/app/build.gradle.kts   ← compileOptions { sourceCompatibility = VERSION_17 }
      │
      ▼
Gradle configures the project  ← AGP extension holds the resolved value
      │
      ▼
updateAndroidVersions task ──▶ compileOptions.sourceCompatibility ──▶ "17"
```

Extending that task with `compileOptions.sourceCompatibility.majorVersion` (with the
same dual-DSL fallback already written for `buildToolsVersion`, and a `?: error(...)`
so it fails loudly) reads exactly what `flutter create` produced. It tracks Flutter
automatically if the template ever moves to 21.

**Candidates rejected, with reasons:**

| Candidate | Why not |
|---|---|
| `flutter doctor` | Reports the *installed* JDK — circular, reproduces today's bug. No `--machine` flag |
| `flutter analyze --suggestions` | Returns a compatibility *verdict*, never a version; and its validator sets `machineOutput => false`, so it is excluded from `--machine` output entirely |
| `DEPS` | Wrong semantics (F6) — would silently move the image to 21 |
| `releases_linux.json` | Contains no Java key |
| Grepping the template `.tmpl` file | Same value, but regex-on-source; three templates exist and could diverge |

**Open design questions:**

1. **Does the Dockerfile pin follow automatically, or does it gate?** The major
   version is welded into the ARG *name* (`OPENJDK_17_JDK_HEADLESS_VERSION`), so a
   17→21 move is a rename plus a suite change, not a value bump. Cleanest: derive
   `version.json`, and have CI fail loudly if the shipped major diverges — leaving
   the actual migration a deliberate human change.
2. **Should `readme.md` show Java?** It currently never mentions it. Once
   `version.json` is a real declaration, publishing it is nearly free.

### F6b — Superseded: openjdk-21's sibling constraint

designed, fix the one that was switched off.

**Item 3 → migrate to openjdk-21, but on corrected grounds.** Not because it
removes the strict-sibling hazard (F6: it does not), but because it collapses two
suite sets into one and retires the entire bookworm special case. If it proceeds,
fix `JAVA_HOME` (`android.Dockerfile:140`) in the same change — it is the one
Java representation with no guard at all, and a migration is exactly when an
unguarded hand-typed path breaks.

**Sequencing:** item 3 makes item 2's Option C nearly trivial (one suite set, no
special case, nothing to cross-check at seam 8). If both are wanted, do 3 first.

The deeper structural finding — that "which Debian release this image is built on"
is stated ~21 times across 4 files and *defined nowhere*, while `config/version.json`
models Flutter/Android/Fastlane/Windows but has no Debian concept at all
(`config/schema.cue:41-57`) — is what makes item 3 expensive to *scope* rather
than to *do*. Recommend a separate change; it is not blocking either item here.

---

## Open Questions

1. **Why is `mode=silent` set, and was it intentional?** The log proves *that* it
   is set and that it comes from Mend's per-repository settings (absent from the
   repo config and from the log's `File`/`CLI`/`Env` config objects). Timing —
   PR #528 opened 2026-08-06, silent run 2026-08-07 — suggests it was switched on
   during the #529 incident. Whether that was deliberate, and whether anything
   still depends on it, is a maintainer/portal question not answerable from the
   repo or the log.

2. **Is the JDK the published image offers part of its contract?** `readme.md`
   never mentions Java (grepped), and `config/version.json.android.java` feeds only
   an internal test — so nothing *documents* JDK 17 to users. But downstream
   Flutter/AGP builds consume it at runtime. Maintainer call; not findable in code
   or on the web.

---

## Next Steps

**Do this first, before any proposal:** turn off `mode=silent` at
[developer.mend.io/github/gmeligio/flutter-docker-image](https://developer.mend.io/github/gmeligio/flutter-docker-image).
It is a portal toggle, it needs no change proposal, and it unblocks both #531's
acceptance test and the two withheld updates. Then file a comment on #532
recording F2 — the issue's stated root cause ("debug level only") is wrong, and
the correction matters for anyone reading it later.

Then run `/opsx:propose` for either:

- **`loud-deb-pin-resolution`** — item 2 as Option C only (this directory); Option
  A is a portal toggle, not a change, or
- **`openjdk-21-migration`** — item 3, which shrinks the above.

Recommend proposing the openjdk-21 migration first. Separately, consider an
upstream docs PR to renovatebot/renovate for the `{{#if release}}` example (F7).

2. **Should `readme.md` publish the Java version?** It currently never mentions
   Java (grepped), so nothing documents JDK 17 to users, though downstream
   Flutter/AGP builds consume it at runtime. Once F8 makes `version.json` a real
   declaration, publishing it is nearly free. Maintainer call.

3. **Does the Dockerfile pin follow the derived value automatically, or gate on
   it?** The major version is welded into the ARG *name*
   (`OPENJDK_17_JDK_HEADLESS_VERSION`), so a future 17→21 move is a rename plus a
   suite change, not a value bump. Recommended shape in F8: derive `version.json`,
   fail CI loudly on divergence, keep the migration itself a deliberate human
   change. Needs a design pass.

4. **Not verified: does Mend's hosted app honour repo-level `mode`?** Precedence is
   stated as design intent in
   [renovatebot/renovate#26724](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/issues/26724)
   ("if the user configures mode=remediation in renovate.json then it would override
   anything set by the app in global config") and matches Mend's documented
   "set `mode: full` in the repos you want to go full" pattern. The next job log
   settles it: if it still reports `mode=silent` after the config merges, Mend is
   forcing the value and the portal is the only lever.

---

Settled decisions: **stay on openjdk-17** (F6), **derive the Java version from the
live `flutter create` toolchain** (F8), **continue PR #531**, **`mode: full` in
`.github/renovate.json`**, **no upstream docs PR** (note it in #531 instead).

Recommended sequence:

| # | Change | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `"mode": "full"` in `.github/renovate.json` | Small PR, on branch `renovate/reconfigure`. Unblocks everything below |
| 2 | Merge PR #531 | After edits above; its acceptance test is now observable |
| 3 | Derive Java version (F8) | Extend `updateAndroidVersions.gradle.kts`; delete `script/java_version.sh` and the backwards workflow step; fix `JAVA_HOME` |
| 4 | `renovate/reconfigure` rule in `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` | Convention, not a gate |

Also worth doing once: comment on #532 recording F2 — the issue's stated root cause
("logged at debug level only") is wrong, and the correction matters for anyone
reading it later.

Then run `/opsx:propose` for **`flutter-java-version-derivation`** (item 3 above —
the substantive change). This directory's item-2 work reduces to `mode: full`, which
is small enough to fold into that proposal or ship on its own.

`research.md` is updated (485 lines). Here's what changed and my answer on #531.

## Should you continue #531?

**Continue it.** It's clean, mergeable, up to date with main, 12 checks green.

Two reasons the Java decision *strengthens* it rather than weakening it:

1. **Its bug is live and independent.** All nine pins resolve against `suite=stable`, which follows whatever Debian calls stable. When Debian 14 ships, all nine silently retarget — the exact mechanism that broke you when trixie replaced bookworm.

2. **Staying on 17 makes bookworm permanent.** Earlier, the openjdk-21 migration would have deleted the bookworm pin and made #531's special-case rule moot. Now it's a permanent requirement.

Two edits before merging:
- Strike the "consider openjdk-21" follow-up — now decided against, with the reasoning recorded so it isn't re-litigated.
- Add the note you asked for: the `{{#if release }}` example came from Renovate's own deb docs. No upstream PR.

And its acceptance test can't be observed until `mode: full` lands, so sequence that first.

## What changed in research.md

- **Headline** now leads with the two settled decisions: stay on 17, derive the version.
- **F6** rewritten with the three-source table — floor (17), template (**17**), and Flutter's `DEPS` (21, its *engine CI formatter* JDK). I explicitly recorded my earlier "de-facto blessed" reading as a correction, since it was wrong and it drove the previous recommendation.
- **F6b** (new) — the derivation design: the `flutter create` → Gradle → AGP-extension chain, plus the four rejected candidates with reasons.
- **F7** — Java's five representations and which are guarded (`JAVA_HOME`: nothing).
- **Recommendation** — #531 continue-not-close, and the `renovate/reconfigure` enforcement caveat.
- **Open Questions** now includes the one thing I haven't verified: whether Mend's hosted app actually honours repo-level `mode`. It's design intent from [#26724](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/issues/26724), and the next job log settles it.

## Sequence

| # | Change |
|---|---|
| 1 | `"mode": "full"` → branch `renovate/reconfigure` |
| 2 | Merge #531 (after the two edits) |
| 3 | Java derivation + delete `java_version.sh` + fix `JAVA_HOME` |
| 4 | `renovate/reconfigure` rule in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md |

Step 3 is the substantive one and wants a proper design pass — mainly the open question of whether the Dockerfile pin *follows* the derived value or just *gates* on it, since the major version is welded into the ARG name.

Want me to run `/opsx:propose` for that, or draft the #531 edits first?
